builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
summary: This is a diagnostic methodology rather than a compression technique: it replaces the assumption that pruning or quantization degrades all capabilities uniformly by measuring per-task fragility under cheap random perturbations and using it to forecast which short-answer capabilities a compressed model will lose first. It costs a perturbation-based evaluation pass plus four-task calibration per deployment, with no extra inference latency or memory in the deployed model. It can fail when profiles are transferred across quantization methods such as GPTQ, when tasks are long-form rather than short-answer, and when the production task distribution differs from the calibrated set.
rationale: For a team shipping quantized or pruned models on a single GPU, a low-cost pre-deployment probe of which capabilities compression will remove is directly actionable, but its predictive validity must be re-verified against the team's own model family, compression method, and task formats before adoption.
technique: Fragility profiling to predict compression-induced capability loss

claims.statement: This is a diagnostic methodology rather than a compression technique: it replaces the assumption that pruning or quantization degrades all capabilities uniformly by measuring per-task fragility under cheap random perturbations and using it to forecast which short-answer capabilities a compressed model will lose first. It costs a perturbation-based evaluation pass plus four-task calibration per deployment, with no extra inference latency or memory in the deployed model. It can fail when profiles are transferred across quantization methods such as GPTQ, when tasks are long-form rather than short-answer, and when the production task distribution differs from the calibrated set.

Fragility profiles from random perturbation, with four-task calibration, predicted held-out post-compression task accuracy with median absolute error 0.11-0.12 versus 0.20-0.21 for a uniform-decline baseline; capability failure order correlated at median 0.90 across perturbation types and 0.875 within-model across pruning and quantization.
